original_question: Does there exist an integer N0 and an N0-tuple S of points in the Euclidean plane such that, for every N, there is a geodesic net whose set of unbalanced vertices is exactly S and whose number of balanced vertices is greater than N? Moreover, do such N0-tuples S form a subset of (R^2)^N0 of positive measure, or even a non-empty open subset?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 3.3.1 in §3.3, “Geodesic nets in the plane: can one bound the number of balanced vertices in terms of the number of unbalanced vertices?”, together with the standing conventions from §1.1 that make the question nontrivial. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the official conjecture very closely: it asks for a fixed integer N0 and a fixed N0-tuple S of points in the Euclidean plane such that, for every N, there exists a geodesic net whose unbalanced vertex set is exactly S and whose number of balanced vertices is greater than N; it also correctly includes the second clause asking whether such S form a subset of (R^2)^N0 of positive measure, or even a non-empty open subset. It also correctly targets geodesic nets rather than geodesic multinets. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))
missing_details: The paper works under standing conventions that suppress the trivial degree-2 phenomenon: no balanced vertex is isolated, degree-2 balanced vertices are regarded as inessential because they can be inserted or removed by subdividing edges, and thereafter all balanced vertices under consideration are taken to have degree at least 3. Without this, the question would not be stand-alone. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))

A geodesic net in the Euclidean plane means a connected embedded straight-edge network with distinct edges and multiplicity 1; geodesic multinets are a different notion allowing intersections/self-intersections and integer edge multiplicities. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))
The paper also imposes the convention that the nets considered contain no edges directly joining two unbalanced vertices. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))

The quantifiers should explicitly say that S is fixed once and for all, independent of N, and that N ranges over positive integers, so the claim is about arbitrarily large finite numbers of balanced vertices. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))

The second clause lives in the standard Euclidean measure/topology on (R^2)^N0: the paper asks for a subset of positive measure, or even a non-empty open subset, of such N0-tuples. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))
refined_question: Under the paper’s standing conventions for geodesic nets in the Euclidean plane—namely, connected embedded nets with straight multiplicity-one edges, no self-intersections or crossings except at common endpoints, no edges between unbalanced vertices, and with degree-2 balanced vertices suppressed so that all counted balanced vertices are non-isolated and have degree at least 3—does there exist an integer N0 and a fixed N0-tuple S in (R^2)^N0 such that for every integer N >= 1 there exists a geodesic net whose set of unbalanced vertices is exactly S and whose number of balanced vertices exceeds N? Moreover, does the collection of such N0-tuples S contain a subset of positive Lebesgue measure in (R^2)^N0, or even a nonempty open subset?
justification: This is essentially verbatim Conjecture 3.3.1. The paragraph immediately before the conjecture explains why it has exactly these two parts: the authors describe evidence from their construction suggesting that the variable part of the unbalanced set might be eliminated and that the remaining constant unbalanced points might persist under small perturbations, which motivates both the fixed-S clause and the positive-measure/open-subset clause. The §1.1 conventions must be imported because otherwise one could create arbitrarily many degree-2 balanced vertices by subdividing edges, making the question artificially easy. Section 4 provides only suggestive/conditional evidence through the 14-point “star” construction and Conjecture 4.5.8; it is not the exact formal statement your draft is aiming at. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1904.00483))
